sections.html:
• Also known as the banana lily or aquatic banana plant.
  • Native to slow-moving waters in the southeastern United States.
  • Beginner-friendly, low light plant.
  • Height of about 6 inches (15 cm).
  • Temperature: 68 to 82°F (20 to 28°C).
  • No CO2 injection needed.

Banana plants are very hardy and easy to care for, with a moderate growth rate that won't get out of control. They prefer tropical temperatures between 68 to 82°F (20 to 28°C) and can survive in low to high light conditions. The more light you give it, the faster it will grow.

No carbon dioxide (CO2) injection is needed, but the plant will appreciate a good all-in-one liquid fertilizer and a root tab inserted right underneath the plant every three to four months.

Once the plant becomes well-established, it will start sending long shoots toward the surface. These shoots grow into heart-shaped leaves that look like lily pads and, in some cases, little white flowers. Prune the floating leaves if needed so they don't block out all the light from other plants.

Sometimes the tubers will melt away and disappear after planting. There are several theories as to why this happens, for example the plant may no longer need the tubers if it gets enough nutrients from the roots. If the plant looks healthy and is still growing, there is no cause for concern.

Planting: Make sure the aquarium has at least two inches (about 5 cm) of substrate, such as aquarium gravel or sand. Choose an area with good lighting and gentle water flow. At six inches (15 cm) tall, this species can be used as a foreground or midground plant, or even as a background plant in a 5-gallon (about 19 litre) nano tank.

Do not suffocate the tubers, the banana-shaped roots used for nutrient storage. Rest the tubers on top of the substrate, or plant them about a quarter of an inch (about 0.6 cm) into the substrate. If the plant tries to float away, use rocks or plant weights to keep it down. If it still won't stay put, it will eventually send down long roots to attach itself to the ground.

Propagation: Cut off one of the leaves and let it float in the tank. Eventually new roots and small leaves will appear, and it can then be planted back into the substrate.
